title: How do you handle a poison-pill message that keeps failing (dead letter topic)?
shortTitle: Handling a poison-pill message that keeps failing (dead letter topic)

s1_definition.profdef: A poison-pill message is a record that a consumer can never successfully process, so every retry fails and, because Kafka does not advance the offset past a record that is not acknowledged, the consumer gets stuck reprocessing the same record forever and blocks the whole partition. The standard remedy is a dead letter topic: after a bounded number of failed attempts, the consumer publishes the problematic record, along with error metadata, to a separate dead letter topic, commits the offset to move past it, and continues processing the rest of the partition. The poison pill is then investigated and replayed offline.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's settlement clerk processing a stack of transfer slips one by one. One slip is garbage the clerk cannot read, and the rule says do not move to the next slip until this one is done. The clerk is now stuck forever on the bad slip while the whole stack waits. A dead letter topic is like a labeled "problem tray": after a few honest tries, the clerk drops the bad slip into the problem tray, notes why, and moves on to the rest of the stack. A supervisor later inspects the problem tray and decides what to do.
s1_definition.oneliner: A poison pill blocks the partition forever on a record that can never succeed, so after bounded retries you route it to a dead letter topic, commit past it, and keep the partition flowing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A poison-pill message is a record that a consumer can never successfully process, so every retry fails and, because Kafka does not advance the offset past a record that is not acknowledged, the consumer gets stuck reprocessing the same record forever and blocks the whole partition. The standard remedy is a dead letter topic: after a bounded number of failed attempts, the consumer publishes the problematic record, along with error metadata, to a separate dead letter topic, commits the offset to move past it, and continues processing the rest of the partition. The poison pill is then investigated and replayed offline.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's settlement clerk processing a stack of transfer slips one by one. One slip is garbage the clerk cannot read, and the rule says do not move to the next slip until this one is done. The clerk is now stuck forever on the bad slip while the whole stack waits. A dead letter topic is like a labeled "problem tray": after a few honest tries, the clerk drops the bad slip into the problem tray, notes why, and moves on to the rest of the stack. A supervisor later inspects the problem tray and decides what to do.

**One line to remember:** A poison pill blocks the partition forever on a record that can never succeed, so after bounded retries you route it to a dead letter topic, commit past it, and keep the partition flowing.

sections.s2_technical:
First understand why a poison pill blocks everything. A Kafka consumer processes records in offset order and only commits the offset after successful handling. If a record throws every time, the consumer never commits past it. On the next poll or restart it fetches the same record and fails again, an endless loop. Because a partition is single-threaded per consumer, that one record stalls every record behind it on that partition.

The core fix is a dead letter topic, often called a dead letter queue. You wrap processing in a bounded retry: try the record, and if it fails up to a configured number of times, stop retrying, produce the original record plus metadata, such as the exception message, stack trace, original topic, partition, offset, and timestamp, to a dead letter topic like `transfers.DLT`, then commit the offset so the consumer advances. The partition keeps flowing and the problem is isolated rather than fatal.

In Spring Kafka this is first-class. You configure a `DefaultErrorHandler` with a `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer` and a `BackOff`, for example `new DefaultErrorHandler(new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(kafkaTemplate), new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3))`, which retries three times with a one-second wait and then publishes to the dead letter topic named after the original with a `.DLT` suffix. You should classify exceptions: some, like a transient database timeout, are retryable, while others, like a deserialization or validation failure, are not retryable and should go straight to the dead letter topic without wasting retries. Spring lets you mark exceptions as not retryable with `addNotRetryableExceptions`.

The senior nuances are these. The dead letter record must carry enough context to debug and replay, so include the headers Spring adds automatically plus a correlation id. A poison pill is frequently a deserialization failure, in which case a safe or error-handling deserializer is needed so the consumer does not crash before the error handler even runs. You must monitor the dead letter topic, because an unwatched dead letter topic becomes a silent graveyard where failures pile up unnoticed. And a dead letter topic is not a fix by itself; it is an isolation mechanism that must be paired with alerting, root-cause classification, and a replay procedure. Finally, consumers should be idempotent so that when you eventually replay a dead letter record, you do not cause duplicate side effects.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's settlement consumer reads transfer events. One day a producer bug emits a record with a negative amount that fails validation. The consumer throws, never commits past it, and every record behind it on that partition stops settling. This is exactly the poison-pill partition stall.

Problem 2 — The team adds a bounded retry with a dead letter topic. The bad record is retried a few times, then published to `transfers.DLT` with the error details, and the consumer commits and moves on, so the rest of the partition settles normally. This is exactly how a dead letter topic isolates a poison pill.

We simulate this in plain Java. A `SettlementConsumer` processes records, validates them, retries up to three times, and on exhaustion sends to a `DeadLetterTopic` with metadata, then advances. The demo feeds a good record, a poison record, and another good record to show the poison one is quarantined while the others succeed. The code will show: a `TransferRecord`, a `ValidationException`, a `DeadLetterTopic`, the `SettlementConsumer` with retry and recovery, and a demo.

```yaml
# application.yml — Spring Kafka dead letter handling
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement
      enable-auto-commit: false
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
# DefaultErrorHandler + DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer is wired in Java config:
#   new DefaultErrorHandler(new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template),
#                           new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3))
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a partition with three records at offsets 10, 11, and 12, where offset 11 has a negative amount and is the poison pill.

Step 1: The consumer reads offset 10, a valid fifty-thousand transfer. Settlement succeeds, the consumer commits offset 10, and the settled count becomes one.

Step 2: The consumer reads offset 11, a transfer with amount minus ninety-nine. Validation throws a ValidationException. Because that exception is classified as non-retryable, the consumer does not retry; a negative amount will never become valid.

Step 3: The consumer publishes the offset-11 record to the dead letter topic with the error message and the attempt count, then advances the committed offset to 11. The partition is no longer blocked.

Step 4: The consumer reads offset 12, a valid twenty-thousand transfer. Settlement succeeds, it commits offset 12, and the settled count becomes two.

Step 5: At the end, two records settled successfully, the committed offset is 12 so nothing is stuck, and the dead letter topic holds exactly one record describing the poison pill, ready for a supervisor to inspect and replay after the producer bug is fixed.

```
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Settled offset=10 SAV2001->CUR3001 50000, committed offset=10
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [SEVERE ] Non-retryable failure for offset=11 SAV2001->CUR3001 -99: amount must be positive, got -99
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [WARNING] Routed to transfers.DLT, committed offset=11
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Settled offset=12 CUR3001->SAV2001 20000, committed offset=12
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Settled OK = 2, final committed offset = 12
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] Dead letters:
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ]   DLT{offset=11 SAV2001->CUR3001 -99, from=transfers, attempts=1, error='amount must be positive, got -99'}
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A poison-pill message is a record a consumer can never process successfully, and the danger is that it blocks the entire partition. Kafka processes records in offset order and only commits after success, so if one record fails every time, the consumer never advances past it, refetches it on every poll, and fails again forever, stalling every record behind it on that single-threaded partition. In a bank that means settlement for a whole partition grinds to a halt because of one bad record.

The standard remedy is a dead letter topic. I wrap processing in a bounded retry: try the record a configured number of times, and if it still fails, publish the original record plus error metadata, such as the exception, stack trace, original topic, partition, offset, and a correlation id, to a dead letter topic like transfers.DLT, then commit the offset so the consumer moves on. The partition keeps flowing and the problem is isolated instead of fatal. In Spring Kafka this is a DefaultErrorHandler with a DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer and a backoff, and I classify exceptions so that a transient database timeout is retried while a validation or deserialization failure, which will never succeed, goes straight to the dead letter topic without wasting retries.

The senior points I always add are that the dead letter record must carry enough context to debug and replay, that deserialization poison pills need a safe deserializer so the consumer does not crash before the error handler runs, and that a dead letter topic is only an isolation mechanism, not a solution. Without monitoring on its depth, root-cause classification, a replay procedure, and clear ownership, it quietly becomes a graveyard where failures accumulate unseen. I also keep consumers idempotent so that when I eventually replay a dead letter record, I do not create duplicate side effects.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, a producer bug once emitted a transfer with a negative amount, and before we had this in place it stalled an entire settlement partition. We added bounded retries with a dead letter topic, so now a non-retryable validation failure is quarantined to transfers.DLT with full error context, the consumer commits past it, and the rest of the partition settles normally. We alert on dead letter topic growth, inspect the records to find the root cause, fix the producer, and then redrive the quarantined records safely because our consumers are idempotent. The senior framing I give is that handling a poison pill well is the difference between one bad record causing a localized, observable, recoverable event and that same record silently taking down settlement for a whole partition.

---

keyPoints: Dead Letter Topic (DLT): store failed messages for later analysis
Retry topic: automatic retry with backoff before DLT
Poison pill: message that always fails — skip or DLT
